vignette:
Henry Thompson, a 68-year-old school counselor, had always been a source of support and guidance for his students. His calm demeanor and approachable nature made him a trusted figure within the community. However, for the past two years, a shadow had crept over his life, entwined with the memory of a traumatic event that had shattered his sense of safety. The assault occurred one evening while he was walking home after late meetings at school. An unexpected confrontation left him feeling powerless and terrified, the adrenaline coursing through him as he fought to escape. In the aftermath, Henry found himself grappling with sensations that echoed the trauma, often triggered by the most innocuous moments.

Certain smells began to haunt Henry. The antiseptic odor of hospitals, reminiscent of a sterile environment where he had been treated after the assault, would engulf him unexpectedly. The moment the scent hit him, it was as if a door had swung open in his mind, unleashing a torrent of vivid memories from that night, each one more terrifying than the last. The smell of antiseptic would send him spiraling back to the hospital, where the memories of the assault flooded his mind with an intensity that felt all too real, as if he were reliving the terror in real time. Each time the antiseptic odor enveloped him, the memories would flood back in vivid detail, bringing with them sensations of panic and fear that paralyzed him, making it impossible to escape the grip of those haunting moments. Each time the antiseptic odor enveloped him, he was transported back to the hospital, where every detail of the assault replayed in his mind with stark clarity, making it impossible for him to escape the grip of those haunting moments. Even now, the scent would seize him, pulling him back to that dreadful night, flooding him with an overwhelming sense of terror, as if he were reliving the experience in vivid detail. In addition, the smell of alcohol triggered another wave of distress, each whiff conjuring memories of the assailant, who had been under the influence at the time. These olfactory triggers would flood his mind with snapshots of the horrifying event; he could recall specific moments—the glint of a blade, the rush of footsteps—etched into his memory like haunting photographs. Each recollection felt as vivid as the original event, and Henry often found himself unable to shake the terror that accompanied these memories.

In an attempt to cope with the relentless waves of anxiety brought on by these triggers, Henry developed maladaptive strategies. He found himself deliberately dissociating, trying to retreat from his body during moments of distress, almost as if it were a protective mechanism to distance himself from the overwhelming feelings. The memories, especially when they surfaced unexpectedly, would paralyze him with fear. He had learned that when these memories emerged, the only way to cope was to retreat into a mental fog, believing that by dissociating, he could shield himself from the overwhelming sensations that accompanied those recollections. The memories, particularly those that surfaced unexpectedly, became so distressing that Henry found himself resorting to dissociation as a protective strategy, convinced that detaching from the moment was the only way to escape the panic they triggered. The memories would often paralyze him with fear, leading Henry to develop this dissociative strategy as a way to avoid the panic that surged with each recollection, convincing himself that detaching was his only escape. He had learned that when these memories emerged, the only way to cope was to retreat into a mental fog, believing that by dissociating, he could shield himself from the overwhelming sensations that accompanied those recollections. In those moments of overwhelming panic, Henry had learned to retreat into a mental fog, believing that if he could detach himself from the sensations, he might escape the haunting images that flooded his mind. Henry could feel the terror wash over him again, making him retreat into a mental fog. This dissociation became a habit; a way to blank out the panic that arose with the memories, yet it left him feeling even more disconnected from the world around him. He started avoiding social gatherings, convinced that being around others would only heighten his anxiety and lead to situations where triggers might arise. Each time he chose to sidestep an invitation, he crafted a tighter web of avoidance, which in turn heightened his sensitivity to the triggers he so desperately wanted to evade, creating a world filled with reminders of his trauma. His pattern of avoidance had begun to map out his life, as the places he no longer visited and the people he kept at arm's length became constant reminders of his fear, reinforcing the very triggers he sought to escape. The more he engaged in avoidance, the more he felt the world closing in around him, leaving him with fewer options and increasing the anxiety that came with each encounter, as if his retreat had drawn a map of reminders he could no longer escape. Each time he sidestepped an invitation, he felt a sense of relief, but with that relief came the creeping realization that the more he distanced himself, the more he crafted a life filled with invisible barriers against the very world that had once brought him joy. Yet, as he avoided social interactions, each place he no longer visited and every person he kept at arm's length became a constant reminder of his trauma, reinforcing the very triggers he sought to evade and tightening the grip of his isolation.

As months turned into years, Henry’s avoidance spiraled into a profound sense of isolation. He found himself steering clear of emotional closeness with his wife, Mary, who yearned for a deeper connection. He could see the longing in her eyes, but the thought of being intimate or vulnerable felt like standing on the edge of a precipice, ready to fall back into the abyss of his trauma. The fear of being emotionally close to anyone, including Mary, became a self-fulfilling prophecy. He created distance, believing that if he kept his walls high, he could prevent the triggers from surfacing, yet he only seemed to push the people he loved further away.

Henry's world continued to shrink, with social interactions dwindling to the bare minimum. He felt as though he was trapped in a cycle—his memories were triggered by scents, which led to maladaptive strategies that further entrenched him in avoidance, only to loop back to the very triggers he sought to evade. The isolation began to weigh heavily on him, and he could see the toll it was taking on his marriage and his own mental health. 

Finally, after months of spiraling, Henry mustered the courage to seek help. He realized he could no longer allow the memories to dictate his life, nor could he continue to let fear rob him of the love and companionship he cherished. What frightened him most was the possibility that he might never regain the closeness he once had with Mary or the joy he felt in his work. As he sat in the waiting room of the therapist’s office, he felt a mix of hope and dread. He wanted to believe in the possibility of healing, yet the fear of facing the memories and the feelings they evoked felt like an insurmountable barrier. The moment the scent hit him, he would be flooded with flashbacks of the hospital, where every detail of the assault replayed in his mind with stark clarity, leaving him feeling trapped in the terror of those moments.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Memory: The relationship between triggers and memory is not clearly established, as the vignette does not explicitly state that the triggers directly lead to the intrusive memories that Henry experiences.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette fails to demonstrate that the memories lead to the development of maladaptive strategies, missing the causal connection between the intrusive memories and the coping mechanisms employed by Henry.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The causal relationship between maladaptive strategies and triggers is not conveyed, as it does not indicate that Henry's avoidance behaviors are a direct result of the triggers he encounters.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Henry Thompson, a 68-year-old school counselor, had always been a source of support and guidance for his students. His calm demeanor and approachable nature made him a trusted figure within the community. However, for the past two years, a shadow had crept over his life, entwined with the memory of a traumatic event that had shattered his sense of safety. The assault occurred one evening while he was walking home after late meetings at school. An unexpected confrontation left him feeling powerless and terrified, the adrenaline coursing through him as he fought to escape. In the aftermath, Henry found himself grappling with sensations that echoed the trauma, often triggered by the most innocuous moments.

Certain smells began to haunt Henry. The antiseptic odor of hospitals, reminiscent of a sterile environment where he had been treated after the assault, would engulf him unexpectedly. The moment the scent hit him, it was as if a door had swung open in his mind, unleashing a torrent of vivid memories from that night, each one more terrifying than the last. Each time the antiseptic odor enveloped him, the memories would flood back in vivid detail, bringing with them sensations of panic and fear that paralyzed him, making it impossible to escape the grip of those haunting moments. Each time the antiseptic odor enveloped him, he was transported back to the hospital, where every detail of the assault replayed in his mind with stark clarity, making it impossible for him to escape the grip of those haunting moments. Even now, the scent would seize him, pulling him back to that dreadful night, flooding him with an overwhelming sense of terror, as if he were reliving the experience in vivid detail. In addition, the smell of alcohol triggered another wave of distress, each whiff conjuring memories of the assailant, who had been under the influence at the time. These olfactory triggers would flood his mind with snapshots of the horrifying event; he could recall specific moments—the glint of a blade, the rush of footsteps—etched into his memory like haunting photographs. Each recollection felt as vivid as the original event, and Henry often found himself unable to shake the terror that accompanied these memories.

In an attempt to cope with the relentless waves of anxiety brought on by these triggers, Henry developed maladaptive strategies. He found himself deliberately dissociating, trying to retreat from his body during moments of distress, almost as if it were a protective mechanism to distance himself from the overwhelming feelings. The memories, especially when they surfaced unexpectedly, would paralyze him with fear. He had learned that when these memories emerged, the only way to cope was to retreat into a mental fog, believing that by dissociating, he could shield himself from the overwhelming sensations that accompanied those recollections. The memories would often paralyze him with fear, leading Henry to develop this dissociative strategy as a way to avoid the panic that surged with each recollection, convincing himself that detaching was his only escape. He had learned that when these memories emerged, the only way to cope was to retreat into a mental fog, believing that by dissociating, he could shield himself from the overwhelming sensations that accompanied those recollections. In those moments of overwhelming panic, Henry had learned to retreat into a mental fog, believing that if he could detach himself from the sensations, he might escape the haunting images that flooded his mind. Henry could feel the terror wash over him again, making him retreat into a mental fog. This dissociation became a habit; a way to blank out the panic that arose with the memories, yet it left him feeling even more disconnected from the world around him. He started avoiding social gatherings, convinced that being around others would only heighten his anxiety and lead to situations where triggers might arise. Each time he chose to sidestep an invitation, he crafted a tighter web of avoidance, which in turn heightened his sensitivity to the triggers he so desperately wanted to evade, creating a world filled with reminders of his trauma. His pattern of avoidance had begun to map out his life, as the places he no longer visited and the people he kept at arm's length became constant reminders of his fear, reinforcing the very triggers he sought to escape. The more he engaged in avoidance, the more he felt the world closing in around him, leaving him with fewer options and increasing the anxiety that came with each encounter, as if his retreat had drawn a map of reminders he could no longer escape. Each time he sidestepped an invitation, he felt a sense of relief, but with that relief came the creeping realization that the more he distanced himself, the more he crafted a life filled with invisible barriers against the very world that had once brought him joy.

As months turned into years, Henry’s avoidance spiraled into a profound sense of isolation. He found himself steering clear of emotional closeness with his wife, Mary, who yearned for a deeper connection. He could see the longing in her eyes, but the thought of being intimate or vulnerable felt like standing on the edge of a precipice, ready to fall back into the abyss of his trauma. The fear of being emotionally close to anyone, including Mary, became a self-fulfilling prophecy. He created distance, believing that if he kept his walls high, he could prevent the triggers from surfacing, yet he only seemed to push the people he loved further away.

Henry's world continued to shrink, with social interactions dwindling to the bare minimum. He felt as though he was trapped in a cycle—his memories were triggered by scents, which led to maladaptive strategies that further entrenched him in avoidance, only to loop back to the very triggers he sought to evade. The isolation began to weigh heavily on him, and he could see the toll it was taking on his marriage and his own mental health. 

Finally, after months of spiraling, Henry mustered the courage to seek help. He realized he could no longer allow the memories to dictate his life, nor could he continue to let fear rob him of the love and companionship he cherished. What frightened him most was the possibility that he might never regain the closeness he once had with Mary or the joy he felt in his work. As he sat in the waiting room of the therapist’s office, he felt a mix of hope and dread. He wanted to believe in the possibility of healing, yet the fear of facing the memories and the feelings they evoked felt like an insurmountable barrier. The moment the scent hit him, he would be flooded with flashbacks of the hospital, where every detail of the assault replayed in his mind with stark clarity, leaving him feeling trapped in the terror of those moments.
